Microphone directionality describes sensitivity to sound arriving from different directions, helping explain which parts of the source and surroundings a recording may capture. Cardioid microphones favor the front, figure-eight microphones capture front and rear while reducing side pickup, and omnidirectional microphones capture broadly from all directions. Shotgun microphones emphasize sound along their axis, although room reflections can still enter the recording. Placement affects the balance between direct sound and room reflections, while microphone angle can change which source details are emphasized. Omnidirectional microphones receive sound broadly, cardioid and shotgun microphones favor their aimed direction, and figure-eight microphones receive from the front and rear while reducing pickup from the sides. Closer placement generally emphasizes direct sound relative to room reflections, while greater distance can make the room more prominent. This batch records microphone pattern and distance, but lacks orientation and detailed room geometry, so those fields cannot establish the exact audible result. A recording description should state the documented setup, distinguish observed sound from expected effects, and keep capture characteristics separate from the exhibit’s material identity.
